strengths: Provides a theoretically grounded approach (Theorem 1) connecting random Fourier feature embeddings of occupancy measures to true MMD distances, giving a principled justification for using these embeddings as behavior representations rather than relying on ad-hoc proxy objectives like state reconstruction.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six continuous control environments against five diverse and relevant baselines (RegularQD, Aurora, LSTM-Aurora, DvD-ES, SMERL), covering hand-crafted, learned, evolutionary, and RL-based diversity approaches.

Uses three complementary evaluation metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, quality-weighted Vendi Score) to mitigate bias toward any single notion of diversity, which is a thoughtful methodological choice given the inherent difficulty of comparing methods with different diversity objectives.

Includes an additional application study (robustness to changed friction/mass dynamics) that demonstrates a practically meaningful benefit of the discovered diverse policy populations, going beyond simple benchmark scores.
Provides ablations on embedding dimension and behavioral descriptor dimension that offer useful insight into the trade-offs of the proposed cwPCA-based descriptor extraction.
Reasonably transparent reporting of failure cases (HalfCheetah, Walker2d) rather than only favorable results, and a candid limitations section.
Detailed appendices with algorithm pseudocode, proof, and hyperparameters that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee (Theorem 1) is derived for the embedding φ^π obtained via i.i.d. geometric-discount sampling, but the paper explicitly switches to a different, more data-efficient embedding ψ^π (Eq. 6) for practical use, without providing a matching theoretical analysis; the link between the proven guarantee and what is actually deployed is only informally motivated (same expectation), leaving a gap between theory and practice.

The dimensionality reduction step (cwPCA) that turns the theoretically-grounded high-dimensional embeddings into low-dimensional behavioral descriptors has no theoretical backing — it is a heuristic combination of fitness-weighted PCA and quantile calibration, so the paper's core practical algorithm is only partially supported by its theoretical contribution.

Only three random seeds are used per environment/method, which is relatively limited for QD-RL and evolutionary strategy experiments known to have high variance; conclusions in close cases (e.g., qVS/VS differences between AutoQD and RegularQD in Walker2d) may not be fully reliable at this sample size.

No comparison to more recent/stronger gradient-based QD methods (e.g., PPGA, DQD, PGA-MAP-Elites) that are cited as state-of-the-art in the related work, despite being readily combinable with the proposed descriptor discovery method; this leaves open whether AutoQD's gains persist with stronger underlying optimizers.

No reporting of computational overhead/wall-clock comparisons between AutoQD and baselines, despite AutoQD requiring periodic RFF-based embedding computation and cwPCA updates, which is relevant for practical adoption alongside Aurora/LSTM-Aurora's autoencoder retraining costs.

The case studies in HalfCheetah and Walker2d suggest that PCA-derived directions of maximal fitness-weighted variance do not necessarily correspond to behaviorally meaningful or interpretable diversity (e.g., 'sliding' policies, over-emphasis on foot joints), suggesting the descriptor discovery may still miss interesting diversity dimensions much like hand-crafted BDs, undercutting part of the motivating claim that automatic descriptors avoid this pitfall.

The kernel bandwidth for the RFF embedding is fixed via a simple heuristic and not ablated or adaptively tuned, which the authors themselves note as a limitation but do not empirically explore, leaving the sensitivity of results to this choice unclear.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuine and well-motivated limitation of QD algorithms: reliance on hand-crafted behavioral descriptors.

The use of occupancy measures as a theoretically complete characterization of policy behavior, combined with random Fourier feature approximations of MMD, is a reasonably principled idea for automatic descriptor discovery.
Theorem 1 provides a convergence guarantee connecting the finite-dimensional embedding distances to the true MMD between occupancy measures, lending some formal grounding to the method.

The empirical evaluation spans six continuous control environments and five diverse baselines (unsupervised QD, RL-based skill discovery, and evolutionary diversity methods), which is a reasonably comprehensive comparison.
The paper attempts to address evaluation fairness by using three different metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, qVS) rather than relying on a single potentially biased measure.
Additional experiments on robustness to changing dynamics (friction/mass) and ablations on embedding/descriptor dimensionality add some depth to the empirical analysis.
Full hyperparameters, pseudocode, and proofs are provided in appendices, aiding reproducibility of the described setup.
weaknesses: The evaluation metrics VS and qVS are computed using a kernel over Random Fourier Feature embeddings that are structurally identical in spirit to the embeddings AutoQD itself optimizes toward, raising a serious concern about circularity: the diversity notion being measured is closely aligned with the method's own inductive bias, which could systematically favor AutoQD over baselines that target different notions of diversity (e.g., hand-crafted BDs, state-based encodings).

The core theoretical contribution (Theorem 1) is largely a composition of existing results (Rahimi & Recht's RFF uniform convergence, Hoeffding's inequality) with fairly loose constants (3/4 ε, exponents with many nested O(·) terms), offering limited new theoretical insight beyond assembling known convergence arguments.

The qualitative failure analyses (e.g., HalfCheetah 'sliding' behaviors, Walker2d overemphasizing foot joints) suggest that the discovered 'diverse' behaviors are not always meaningful or interpretable, undermining the central motivating claim that occupancy-measure-based embeddings yield behaviorally significant descriptors.

The huge margins by which AutoQD outperforms RegularQD on the GT QD Score (e.g., Ant: ~361 vs ~182, ×10^4) seem suspiciously large and are not clearly explained; it is unclear how much of this gain is attributable to the proposed embedding method versus other confounds (e.g., differences in how the archive is filled, interaction with CMA-MAE, or boundary effects of behavior space calibration).

Baseline comparisons mix fundamentally different optimization paradigms (CMA-MAE-based QD methods vs. gradient-based RL methods like SMERL and DvD-ES), confounding the contribution of the proposed embedding with the choice of a more sample-efficient evolutionary optimizer; a fairer ablation would isolate the behavioral descriptor choice while holding the optimizer fixed.

The behavioral descriptor dimensionality (k=4) is fixed somewhat arbitrarily, and the paper's own ablation shows a clear quality-diversity tradeoff with dimensionality without a principled method for choosing k.

The iterative refinement of the affine projection (cwPCA) changes the behavior space over time, but the paper does not clearly address how this affects the consistency of policies already placed in earlier archive cells or whether re-mapping introduces instability.

Experiments are limited to standard MuJoCo/Gymnasium benchmarks already well-covered by established hand-crafted descriptors, which somewhat undercuts the motivation that this method is most valuable for open-ended or complex domains where hand-crafted BDs are infeasible; no such domain is tested.
Only 3 random seeds are used for most results, which is a relatively weak basis for the statistical claims given the variance in QD and RL training.
No mention of code release or public implementation, limiting reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: The paper presents a theoretically grounded approach to automatic behavioral descriptor discovery, exploiting the well-known one-to-one correspondence between policies and occupancy measures and connecting it to MMD via random Fourier features. This gives a principled foundation compared to prior heuristic autoencoder-based approaches (AURORA, LSTM-AURORA).

Theorem 1 provides a rigorous, non-asymptotic finite-sample bound showing convergence of the RFF-based embedding distances to the true MMD between occupancy measures, with a full proof included in the appendix.

The proposed cwPCA (calibrated weighted PCA) mechanism is a simple, well-motivated, and computationally efficient way to derive low-dimensional, archive-compatible descriptors that adapt over the course of optimization, with clear ablations validating design choices (dimension of embeddings and behavior descriptors).

Extensive empirical evaluation across six standard continuous control benchmarks with five competitive baselines (RegularQD, Aurora, LSTM-Aurora, DvD-ES, SMERL) spanning distinct paradigms (unsupervised QD, evolutionary diversity, RL-based skill discovery).

Use of multiple complementary evaluation metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, qVS) to fairly assess methods that optimize different notions of diversity, which is a thoughtful methodological contribution in itself.

An additional experiment on robustness to changing dynamics (friction/mass perturbations) provides a compelling practical demonstration of the value of the discovered diverse policies beyond just archive metrics.

The paper is generally well-written, clearly structured, and includes substantial supplementary material (proofs, algorithm pseudocode, extensive hyperparameter and implementation details) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: AutoQD does not uniformly dominate baselines (e.g., loses to RegularQD/Aurora in Walker2d/HalfCheetah on some metrics), and the paper's post-hoc qualitative explanations (e.g., 'sliding' behaviors, overemphasis on foot joints) are somewhat speculative without deeper quantitative analysis or visualization to substantiate these claims.

The theoretical guarantee (Theorem 1) is about embedding distance approximating MMD, but the practical algorithm uses a different, non-i.i.d. estimator (Eq. 6, using discounted weighted transitions from full trajectories) motivated only heuristically ('same expectation, reduces variance') without a corresponding formal guarantee, creating a gap between theory and the deployed method.

Baseline hyperparameter tuning appears somewhat asymmetric/ad hoc (e.g., differing network sizes, SMERL and DvD-ES using non-Toeplitz architectures or author-default configs primarily copied from original papers), raising some concern about whether baselines were tuned as carefully as the proposed method for these particular tasks/architectures.

Only 3 random seeds are used for the main experiments, which is a relatively small number for stochastic evolutionary/RL methods, potentially limiting the statistical robustness of the reported comparisons despite standard errors being provided.

The dimensionality reduction (cwPCA) step, while practically motivated, is a linear projection of a complex nonlinear behavior space; the paper does not deeply explore whether important behavioral variation is lost through this affine restriction, beyond a limited dimension ablation on a single environment (BipedalWalker).

The kernel bandwidth is fixed rather than adaptively tuned, which the authors themselves note as a limitation that could affect performance across tasks with different reward/state scales, and no sensitivity analysis for this hyperparameter is provided in the main paper.

strengths: Presents a theoretically grounded approach to automatic behavior descriptor discovery, exploiting the well-known policy-occupancy-measure correspondence combined with random Fourier feature approximations of MMD; this gives a principled alternative to heuristic autoencoder-based unsupervised BD methods (Aurora, LSTM-Aurora).

Rigorous theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 with a full, careful proof (including an extension in Appendix B justifying the practical trajectory-averaged embedding used in the algorithm, and even acknowledging finite-horizon truncation bias), giving concrete, non-asymptotic finite-sample/finite-dimension convergence guarantees connecting embedding distances to true MMD between occupancy measures.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six standard continuous-control benchmarks against five diverse and relevant baselines (RegularQD, Aurora, LSTM-Aurora, DvD-ES, SMERL), using multiple complementary QD/diversity metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, quality-weighted Vendi Score), with AutoQD outperforming baselines in most settings.

Extensive and honest ancillary analyses: quality-diversity trade-off scatter plot, fine-grained per-task statistics, adaptation-to-dynamics-shift experiments (friction/mass), ablations on embedding dimension, BD dimension, weighting mechanism, and number of rollouts for descriptor stability, plus qualitative visualization of discovered behaviors -- this thoroughness is a notable strength for reproducibility and understanding of the method's behavior.

Clear, well-motivated method exposition (Fig. 1/2, Algorithm 1) and reasonably complete implementation/hyperparameter details in the appendix; the paper explicitly discusses failure cases (HalfCheetah, Walker2d) and offers plausible explanations rather than hiding weaknesses.

The cwPCA weighting scheme and calibration procedure are practically motivated and empirically ablated, showing the authors considered subtle interactions between the QD algorithm and the learned descriptor space.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee (Theorem 1) is an asymptotic/high-probability bound that requires the trajectory-embeddings to come from i.i.d. samples of the true occupancy measure; the practical implementation (single evaluation batch of n=5 rollouts, fixed kernel bandwidth, fixed random features reused across the entire run in Algorithm 1) may not tightly satisfy the theorem's assumptions, and the paper does not empirically validate how well the theoretical convergence rate is realized in practice (e.g., no plot of embedding-distance vs. ground truth MMD error as n or D scale).

Only 3 random seeds are used for main experiments (Table 1), which is a relatively small sample size for stochastic RL/QD experiments and makes some of the close comparisons (e.g., AutoQD vs. RegularQD in Walker2d, or vs. Aurora in HalfCheetah) statistically weak; no significance tests are reported for the main results table (unlike the cwPCA ablation, which does use Mann-Whitney U).

AutoQD introduces a nontrivial set of extra hyperparameters (embedding dimension D, kernel bandwidth, discount factor for the embedding, descriptor dimension k, update schedule for cwPCA) that are fixed to specific values across all six environments without a systematic sensitivity/robustness study beyond BipedalWalker; it's unclear how transferable these choices are to substantially different domains (e.g., higher-dimensional or image-based observations, acknowledged as future work).

Combining AutoQD with the current SOTA gradient-based QD algorithms (PGA-ME/PPGA) is stated to be 'non-trivial' and left as future work, while PGA-ME with ground-truth descriptors clearly outperforms CMA-MAE-based methods on several metrics (Table 8); this leaves open the question of how competitive AutoQD would be against a truly SOTA QD-RL pipeline rather than only CMA-MAE variants, somewhat limiting the significance of the reported improvements.

The identified failure modes (premature convergence to simple/stable behaviors such as HalfCheetah sliding or Walker2d bottom-joint-only gaits) suggest a fundamental limitation of the low-dimensional occupancy-measure projection approach that is not fully resolved, only mitigated by hand-tuning descriptor dimensionality; the paper acknowledges but does not solve this core exploration issue.

The comparison baselines for skill-discovery/unsupervised RL literature is limited to only SMERL (justified by code availability), omitting DIAYN, DADS, or DoMiNo, which somewhat narrows the empirical positioning of AutoQD relative to the broader unsupervised RL literature discussed in Related Work.

The evaluation metrics themselves (VS, qVS) rely on RFF-based kernel embeddings structurally very similar to those AutoQD itself uses to define its behavior space, which, despite the authors' claim of a 'larger, separate' set of features for fairness, introduces a degree of metric-method alignment that could inflate AutoQD's apparent advantage on diversity metrics compared to methods whose behavior spaces are defined very differently (e.g., hand-crafted RegularQD descriptors).

strengths: Provides a theoretically grounded framework connecting occupancy measures, MMD, and random Fourier features for automatic behavior descriptor generation, including a formal convergence theorem (with detailed appendix proof) and an additional justification (Appendix B) for the practical trajectory-based embedding used in the algorithm.

Extensive experimental evaluation across six continuous-control tasks, five baselines spanning distinct paradigms (hand-crafted BDs, autoencoder/LSTM-based unsupervised BDs, population-diversity ES, and RL-based skill discovery), and three complementary metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, qVS).

Thorough appendix material including ablations on embedding dimension, descriptor dimension, number of rollouts for BD estimation, stability analysis of learned descriptors, and qualitative/visual inspection of discovered behaviors, which strengthens reproducibility and interpretability.

Includes a practically motivated robustness/adaptation experiment (friction and mass perturbations) that demonstrates a tangible benefit of the discovered diverse population beyond the abstract QD score.

The paper is transparent about limitations and failure cases (HalfCheetah and Walker2d), offering plausible explanations (early convergence to stable but simple behavioral modes) rather than hiding negative results.
weaknesses: The headline GT QD Score metric inherently favors methods that produce large archives (AutoQD, RegularQD, Aurora, LSTM-Aurora all generate hundreds-to-thousands of policies via CMA-MAE) versus SMERL/DvD-ES which maintain only ~10 policies; this makes the magnitude of AutoQD's reported QD-score advantage (e.g., 361.43 vs 1.02 x10^4 in Ant) less meaningful without clearer normalization, and the paper does not sufficiently address this asymmetry in the main comparison despite using VS/qVS as partial correction.

Only three random seeds are used for the main results, yielding large standard errors in several cells of Table 1 and the ablation tables, which weakens confidence in some of the reported comparisons, especially in cases where AutoQD is close to or below baselines (HalfCheetah qVS, Walker2d qVS/VS).

Baselines differ substantially in training budget and architecture (e.g., SMERL trained for 1.6x10^7 timesteps with SAC, DvD-ES using much smaller 2-layer-32 MLPs) raising questions about whether comparisons are fully controlled for compute and capacity, beyond simply matching the QD backbone (CMA-MAE) for the QD-based methods.

AutoQD underperforms baselines on two of six environments on the central qVS/VS metrics (HalfCheetah, Walker2d), and the explanation (early convergence to low-dimensional stable behavioral attractors) suggests a non-trivial robustness issue with the method rather than a minor edge case, yet this is relegated largely to an appendix discussion.

The theoretical guarantee (Theorem 1) is a loose, multi-term probabilistic bound whose practical implications for selecting D and n are not clearly connected to the actual experimental hyperparameters (e.g., D=100 is used without explicit justification from the bound), and the practical embedding (ψ) used in experiments is a variant not directly covered by the main theorem but only loosely justified in an appendix, slightly overselling the 'theoretically grounded' framing in the abstract/intro.

The method introduces several additional design choices and hyperparameters (kernel bandwidth, embedding dimension, descriptor dimension, update schedule, fitness-weighted PCA, calibration quantiles) whose joint interaction and sensitivity are only partially explored, and some ablations (e.g., weighting in cwPCA) show statistically insignificant effects, raising questions about which components are actually essential to the method's performance.

Important related unsupervised-RL skill-discovery baselines discussed in the related work (e.g., DIAYN, DADS, DoMiNo) are not included in the empirical comparison, limiting the completeness of the empirical positioning relative to the broader unsupervised RL literature the paper claims to differentiate from.

strengths: Provides a theoretically grounded approach to automatic behavior descriptor discovery in QD-RL, connecting occupancy measures, MMD, and random Fourier features with a formal convergence theorem (Theorem 1), including a careful practical extension (Appendix B) justifying the trajectory-averaged embedding used in practice.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across six diverse continuous control tasks (Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Swimmer, Walker2d, BipedalWalker) against five well-chosen and conceptually distinct baselines (RegularQD, Aurora, LSTM-Aurora, DvD-ES, SMERL).

Uses multiple complementary evaluation metrics (GT QD Score, Vendi Score, quality-weighted Vendi Score) and explicitly discusses the biases/limitations of each metric rather than relying on a single number.

Strong set of ablation studies: embedding dimension, behavior descriptor dimension, weighting mechanism in cwPCA, number of rollouts used for descriptor estimation, and stability analysis of learned descriptors versus baselines.
A compelling downstream application (adaptation to changed friction/mass dynamics) demonstrates practical value of the discovered diverse policies beyond the QD score abstraction.
Honest discussion of failure cases (HalfCheetah, Walker2d) with plausible explanations (early convergence to stable/simple behaviors) and correspondingly honest limitations/future work sections.
Qualitative visualizations of discovered behaviors help ground the abstract embedding-based approach in interpretable robot behaviors.
weaknesses: Only three random seeds are used for the main results, which is relatively low for QD-RL experiments known to have high variance; some reported differences (e.g., Walker2d) may not be robustly significant.

AutoQD is only combined with CMA-MAE; the paper acknowledges combining with gradient-based QD methods (PGA-ME, PPGA) is nontrivial and left to future work, so the reference PGA-ME numbers (Appendix F) using ground-truth BDs do not actually validate AutoQD's compatibility with stronger QD optimizers.

The kernel bandwidth for the random Fourier features is fixed via a simple heuristic (sqrt(state+action dim)) rather than tuned or adapted, and the paper acknowledges this as a limitation without exploring alternatives empirically beyond a brief note.
The theoretical bound in Theorem 1, while rigorous, is complex with multiple additive error terms and no concrete guidance on required sample/embedding sizes for a target accuracy in practice.

AutoQD underperforms on two of six environments (HalfCheetah, Walker2d) with descriptor dimensionality apparently contributing to premature convergence to simple/stable behavioral modes; the ablation exploring this (dimension 1-4) is only conducted on BipedalWalker, not on the two problematic domains where it would be most informative.

Some baselines (DvD-ES, SMERL) underperform by very large margins across most metrics, raising a question of whether hyperparameters/training budgets were adequately matched to make for a fully fair comparison, despite the paper's claims of following default/author settings.
